performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: The first movement, Allegro, of Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622, sets an A major theme for the clarinet among quick runs, low phrases and sudden turns into minor keys. William McColl plays a basset clarinet he built himself, with Abraham Kaplan conducting the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra.

sections.label: Intro · Strings present the theme
sections.mNote: A major phrases pass between strings and winds.

sections.label: A · Clarinet solo entry
sections.mNote: The soloist extends the theme into new melodies and runs.

sections.label: Dev · Solo clarinet theme modulates
sections.mNote: Clarinet phrases modulate beyond the exposition’s close in E major.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme returns in A major
sections.mNote: The clarinet plays the opening melody over quiet strings.

sections.label: Coda · The orchestra finishes in A
sections.mNote: Strings and winds take over the closing phrases.

cues.title: Opening orchestral exposition
cues.text: The strings play the first theme, in A major. The winds soon join, and Mozart sets parts of the tune in canon. The orchestra plays its own exposition before the clarinet’s first independent solo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, pp. 207–211. Calvin Dotsey describes the canon within the opening orchestral exposition: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First solo entry, clarinet
cues.text: The clarinet takes up the opening melody over soft strings. It soon extends the tune with new phrases and runs further than the orchestra’s version does. The wind section rests at the clarinet’s entry.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, first solo from bar 57, p. 211. The solo exposition’s new melodies are discussed by Calvin Dotsey.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sketch for basset horn in G
cues.text: A surviving sketch shows that Mozart first planned the concerto for a basset horn in G. He soon changed to the new basset clarinet in A, which reached the octave below middle C. Stadler played it with great skill.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”: the sketch for a basset horn in G, the basset clarinet in A with the octave below middle C, and Stadler’s playing: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/

cues.title: Written for Anton Stadler
cues.text: Mozart wrote the concerto for Anton Stadler and his extended-range clarinet. The instrument’s extra low notes let the solo part descend below the ordinary clarinet’s compass before it climbs back into the upper register.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, on Stadler’s basset clarinet and the concerto’s origin: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/. The performance uses McColl’s self-built basset clarinet: https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.

cues.title: Anton Stadler and Mozart’s money
cues.text: Stadler was a fellow Freemason and a habitual borrower. Mozart’s widow and sister-in-law later said that he never repaid what he borrowed, and that he owed Mozart some 500 florins when Mozart died.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto”, citing comments by Mozart’s widow and sister-in-law (the debt is described as alleged); the accounts were not traced to a primary letter: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/

cues.title: Clarinet accompanying the orchestra
cues.text: Later in the solo exposition the clarinet plays quick broken chords beneath the orchestra’s phrases. Elsewhere in the movement Mozart gives the soloist the melody, or answering phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, later solo exposition, orchestral phrases above the clarinet’s running broken-chord figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development, clarinet entry
cues.text: After the orchestra closes in E major, the clarinet begins the development with a phrase heard earlier in the movement. The harmony then modulates through several keys. In these exchanges the soloist uses both the low and the high ends of its range.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, development following the E major orchestral close; Calvin Dotsey’s account of the first movement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The lost autograph
cues.text: Stadler said that the portmanteau holding Mozart’s manuscripts was stolen in Germany; the widow was told it had been pawned there for 73 ducats. The first edition moved the low passages up an octave for an ordinary clarinet without marking which. Basset clarinettists reconstruct them by educated guesses.
cues.evidence: Constanze Mozart to Johann André, 31 May 1800, in the translation given by Matthew Tift, “Excuse Me, Where Can I Find Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto?” (2002): Stadler “declares that while he was in Germany, his portmanteau, with these pieces in it, was stolen”; others assure her it “was pawned there for 73 ducats”: https://matthewtift.com/sites/default/files/2019-03/2002-02-23-excuse-me-where-can-i-find-mozarts-clarinet-concerto.pdf. The transposed first edition and the attempts at reconstruction: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/

cues.title: McColl’s basset clarinet, 1987
cues.text: In December 1987 William McColl played the concerto on a basset clarinet he had built himself. The University of Washington orchestra accompanied him under Abraham Kaplan.
cues.evidence: The Soni Ventorum archive identifies the performers, date and McColl’s instrument: https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The clarinet plays the opening melody again in A major, with quiet strings around it and first violins replying to the solo line. Mozart leaves the soloist room to elaborate the phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, recapitulation, p. 227.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Prague, 1791
cues.text: The concerto was probably first heard in Prague on 16 October 1791, less than two months before Mozart died at thirty-five. It was the last major instrumental work he completed.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, “Swan Song: Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto” (“likely premiered in Prague on October 16, 1791”; “the last major instrumental composition he composed”): https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/

cues.title: Final ritornello in A major
cues.text: Strings and winds take over the closing phrases in A major. Mozart wrote no large, separate cadenza for this movement. The final orchestral cadence follows the clarinet’s last flourish.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, final ritornello, pp. 234–235. Calvin Dotsey notes the absence of a conventional first-movement cadenza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The clarinet takes the opening tune
transitions.how: The full orchestra closes in A major. Flutes, bassoons and horns then stop, and at bar 57 the clarinet begins its independent solo over quiet strings. The clarinet takes over the familiar melody from the orchestra, and the violins play responses beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, first solo from bar 57, p. 211.

transitions.title: From exposition to development
transitions.how: The orchestra closes the exposition with a cadence in E major. The clarinet re-enters with a phrase heard earlier in the movement, accompanied by lighter strings. Over repeated figures and a moving bass line the solo part leaves E major and leads into the development.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, close of the exposition and opening of the development.

transitions.title: Dominant E leads back to A major
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme returns in A major
transitions.how: The harmony rests on the dominant, E, before the return to A major. The clarinet restores the opening tune over the upper strings at a quiet dynamic. Cellos and double basses rest at its entry. First violins reply to the solo line as the opening phrases return.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, recapitulation, pp. 226–227.

transitions.title: Clarinet flourish into closing ritornello
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme returns in A major
transitions.to: Coda · The orchestra finishes in A
transitions.how: The clarinet’s closing flourish leads into the orchestral ritornello in A major. The winds reinforce the strings, and the scoring then thins briefly before the final full cadence. The movement ends with the full orchestra and no separate cadenza before the close.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, pp. 234–235.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto K. 622, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke XII/20 (1881), plate W.A.M. 622
source.locator: I. Allegro, printed pp. 207–235: orchestral opening, solo entries, development and return. The solo instrument in this performance is McColl’s basset clarinet.

timeline.note: Strings introduce the tune above moving viola, cello and bass parts.
Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings’ opening phrases.
The clarinet plays its first solo above the violins and viola; the lower strings enter later.
The clarinet accompanies the strings with quick broken chords, then takes the melody again.
Winds and strings bring the exposition to its E major close.
The clarinet starts the development over quiet strings.
Strings repeat their figures at changing pitches above sustained bassoon notes.
The clarinet plays the opening tune again above violins and viola; the lower strings enter later.
Winds, horns and strings play the final A major cadence.
The final A major chord has ended.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
